8-1

Lecture 8-1

Where does an enthalpy — and a heat of reaction — actually come from?

Before we add any enthalpies

Enthalpy is only ever a difference

Routes 2 and 3 add enthalpies up. So what does a single enthalpy number actually mean?

$$H = U + PV$$
$U$
internal energy of the system — not measurable on its own
kJ/mol
$PV$
the work of pushing the stream through at pressure $P$
kJ/mol
Enthalpy $H$Heat of formation $\Delta H^{\circ}_f$
What it countstotal heat content, $U+PV$heat to build 1 mol from its elements
Measured alone?no — only changes areyes — by experiment or from a cycle
Its zerochosen, not physicalthe elements, fixed at zero

From the datum to the real state

Every enthalpy is measured from its datum

$$(\Delta) H_i(T,P) = H_i(T,P) - H_{i,\,datum} = \int_{T_{ref}}^{T}\!C^{ig}_{p,i}(T)\,dT + H^{R}_{i}(T,P)$$

Simulators print this as “enthalpy $H_i$” — the $\Delta$ against the datum is implied.

$H_{i,\,datum}$
the value assigned at the reference state
kJ/mol
$C^{ig}_{p,i}$
ideal-gas heat capacity, from a polynomial
kJ/(mol·K)
$H^{R}_{i}$
departure of the real fluid from an ideal gas
kJ/mol
$$H^{R} = \int_{0}^{P}\left[\,V - T\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_{P}\right]dP$$

From an equation of state — Peng–Robinson or SRK. It also carries the latent heat.

Steam table · Aspen HYSYS—

The curves sit 15 971 kJ/kg apart at every temperature, so $\Delta h$ comes out identical.

From the datum to a reaction

Heat of formation / heat of reaction at the standard state

$$\Delta H^{\circ}_{f,i} = \sum_j \nu_j\,\Delta H^{\circ}_{f,j}$$

Species $i$ assembled from the standard formation enthalpies of the species $j$ around it.

$$\mathrm{C(graphite)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2(g)} \qquad \Delta H^{\circ}_{f} = -393.5\ \text{kJ/mol}$$

Standard state = 25 °C, 1 bar; every pure element in its stable form is assigned zero.

Calorimetry

Measure the formation reaction directly in a bomb.

Hess's law

Combine heats of combustion, or a Born–Haber cycle.

Group methods

Benson or Joback, estimated from the structure.

Databases

NIST WebBook, CRC, Perry's, JANAF tables.

Route 1 · the definition

Heat of reaction at the reaction temperature

$$\nu_A A + \nu_B B \rightarrow \nu_C C + \nu_D D \qquad \Delta H_r(T) = \sum_{j=1}^{N}\nu_j H_j(T)$$
$\nu_j$
stoichiometric coefficient of species $j$: negative for a reactant, positive for a product
–
$H_j(T)$
enthalpy of species $j$ at the reaction temperature, referred to the elements
kJ/mol
$\Delta H_r(T)$
heat of reaction per unit of extent at temperature $T$
kJ/mol

Negative $\Delta H_r$ = exothermic, heat comes out. Positive = endothermic.

Route 1 · where $H_j$ starts

The standard state fixes the starting phase

$H_j(T)$ is built from a tabulated value. That table is quoted at one temperature, one pressure and one phase.

$H^{\circ}_{f,j}$
standard enthalpy of formation, from the elements
kJ/mol
$T_R$
the table's reference temperature
25 °C
The value is quoted in the phase that is stable at 25 °C and 1 bar — that is the state the walk starts from.

Toluene and benzene are tabulated as liquids; hydrogen and methane as gases.

Route 1 · from 25 °C to 640 °C

Walking one species up to the reaction temperature

$$H_j(T) = H^{\circ}_{f,j}(T_R) + \Delta H_{vap}(T_R) + \Delta H_{fus}(T_R) + \int_{T_R}^{T}\!C_{p,j}(T)\,dT$$
$\Delta H_{vap}$
latent heat added only if the species must be evaporated
kJ/mol
$C_{p,j}$
heat capacity of species $j$ in the phase it is being heated in
kJ/(mol·K)

Take only the phase changes that actually happen between $T_R$ and $T$.

Interactive · route 1

Three paths, three versions of the same equation

$$H_j = H^{\circ}_{f,j}(T_R) + \underbrace{\Delta H_{vap}}_{\text{only if it evaporates}} + C_p\,(T-T_R)$$
Gas → Gas (kJ/mol)—
Liquid → Gas (kJ/mol)—
Liquid → Liquid (kJ/mol)—

The latent heat is a step, not a slope: it lifts the whole vapour line at once, and for toluene it is worth 145 °C of sensible heating.

Route 1 · putting the species together

The heat of reaction written out

The definition, two slides back$\Delta H_r(T) = \sum_j \nu_j H_j(T)$
$$\text{Liquid}\rightarrow\text{Gas}:\quad \Delta H_r(T) = \Delta H^{\circ}_R(T_R) + \textstyle\sum_j\nu_j C_{p,j}(T-T_R) + \sum_j \nu_j \Delta H_{vap,j}(T_R)$$
$$\text{Same phase throughout}:\quad \Delta H_r(T) = \Delta H^{\circ}_R(T_R) + \textstyle\sum_j\nu_j C_{p,j}(T-T_R)$$

$\Delta H^{\circ}_R(T_R) = \sum_j \nu_j H^{\circ}_{f,j}(T_R)$ — the standard heat of reaction at 25 °C.

Same result either way: enthalpy is a state function, so only the end points matter.

Temperature correction

From 25 °C to the reaction temperature

$$\Delta H_{Rx}(T) = \Delta H^{\circ}_{Rx}(T_R) + \underbrace{\int_{T_R}^{T}\!\Delta C_p\,dT}_{\text{sensible-heat correction}}$$
$$\Delta C_p = \sum_i \nu_i\,C_{p,i}, \qquad C_{p,i} = a_i + b_i T + c_i T^2 + d_i T^3$$

Constant $C_p$ makes the correction linear: $\Delta H_{Rx}(T) \approx \Delta H^{\circ}_{Rx} + \Delta C_p (T-T_R)$.

$a_i, b_i, c_i, d_i$ are the polynomial coefficients printed in property tables.

Getting to the reaction state

Account for phase changes on the way

$$H_i(T) = \Delta H^{\circ}_{f,i} + \int_{T_R}^{T_b}\!C_p^{L}\,dT + \Delta H_{vap} + \int_{T_b}^{T}\!C_p^{G}\,dT$$

$T_b$ = normal boiling point · $\Delta H_{vap}$ = latent heat · $C_p^{L}, C_p^{G}$ = liquid and gas heat capacities.

Fed as liquid but reacting as vapour? Add $\Delta H_{vap}$ at $T_b$ — it often dwarfs both sensible terms.
PathWhat to add
Liquid → Liquidsensible heat only
Liquid → Gassensible heat + $\Delta H_{vap}$
Gas → Gassensible heat only

Interactive · drag the sliders

How $\Delta H_{Rx}$ varies with temperature

From the previous slide$\Delta H_{Rx}(T) = \Delta H^{\circ}_{Rx} + \Delta C_p (T-T_R)$
Value at 300 °C—
Shift over the span—

$\Delta C_p$ only tilts the line. Over a 300 °C span it shifts $\Delta H_{Rx}$ by a few kJ/mol, so the sign — exo or endo — almost never flips.

Route 1 · reading a quoted number

“123 kJ” per what?

$$\Delta H_r = \pm 123\ \frac{\text{kJ}}{\text{mol of limiting reactant}} \qquad \Delta H_r = \pm 456\ \frac{\text{kJ}}{\text{kg of limiting reactant}}$$
  • The basis may be any species in the reaction — the number changes with it.
  • Convention here: per mole of the limiting reactant, whose coefficient is 1.

A heat of reaction without its basis species is unusable.

Lecture 8-1 · summary

What section 8-1 settled

  • Enthalpy has no absolute value — every number is quoted against a chosen datum.
  • On the elemental datum, $H$ at 25 °C is the heat of formation.
  • A standard heat of formation or reaction is built from other $\Delta H^{\circ}_{f}$ values, then corrected to $T$.
  • Across programs only $\Delta h$ is comparable; a single $h$ never is.
8-2

Lecture 8-2

How much heat does this reactor release or absorb?

Lecture 8-2 · the three routes

Three ways to get the same number

1 · Heat of reaction

  • Needs every reaction pathway
  • And each heat of reaction at reaction conditions

2 · Enthalpy difference

  • Outlet enthalpy minus inlet enthalpy
  • No pathway needed

3 · Simulator

  • An isothermal block reports the duty directly
  • Routes 2 and 3 need an isothermal reactor.
  • Route 1 works at any condition.

The case we carry all lecture

Hydrodealkylation (HDA) of toluene to benzene

  • Main reaction (1) makes the benzene we sell.
  • Reactions (2) and (3) convert the feed impurities.
  • Side reaction (4) destroys benzene — it is reversible.

Reaction 3 produces toluene, so toluene appears on both sides of the balance.

Shorthand used from here: T toluene, B benzene, M methane, EB ethylbenzene, X m-xylene, Bi biphenyl.

Route 3 · setup

route 3An isothermal stoichiometric reactor block

Flash type Temperature + Pressure: 640 °C, 35 bar. Duty is left blank — that is what the block returns.

Four reactions, each with its own fractional conversion. Tick “Reactions occur in series” — each conversion then applies to the outlet of the reaction before it, not to the fresh feed. Mind the order: rxn 2 makes toluene before rxn 3 converts 80 % of it.

Reaction 1: reactants carry −1, products +1, then 0.69 fractional conversion of ETHYL-01, its reference component.

Report calculated heat of reaction at 640 °C, 35 bar, phase Vapor — every species is supercritical here, so “liquid” would extrapolate a state that does not exist. It is a reported value: the duty still comes from the enthalpy balance.

Lecture 8-2 · summary

What section 8-2 settled

  • Build $H_j$ from the tabulated formation enthalpy plus every phase change and the sensible heat.
  • Route 1 needs the pathways; route 2 needs only inlet and outlet enthalpies.
  • This reactor releases about 8 000 kW — that number drives everything in section 8-3.
  • Quote a duty with its operating hours, or the kilowatts are meaningless.
8-3

Lecture 8-3

Now that we know the heat load, what hardware absorbs it?

Lecture 8-3 · the vocabulary

Three ways a reactor can be run thermally

Isothermal

  • Inlet and outlet at the same temperature
  • Assumed in kinetics and laboratory work

Adiabatic

  • No heat crosses the wall
  • Hard in a laboratory, easy in a large vessel

Neither

  • Some heat crosses the wall
  • The temperature still moves
  • Most industrial reactors

Ray, S. & Das, G. (2020). Process Equipment and Plant Design, Elsevier.

Lecture 8-3 · the six forms

Six industrial configurations

any of these four — the context decides which
  • An empty vessel: no heat-transfer surface, no utility, no controls — the cheapest and simplest thing to build.
  • Every kJ of reaction leaves as $\Delta T$. Accept it only if the adiabatic rise stays inside the safe, selective window.
  • Rule of thumb, exothermic: the rise is at most 10 % of the inlet temperature, on whichever scale is in use (°C or °F).
  • Each bed is still adiabatic; the temperature is restored in an exchanger between beds, not inside them.
  • $N$ beds cut the rise per bed roughly $N$-fold, paid for with $N-1$ exchangers and extra pressure drop.
  • Rule of thumb: no more than 5 beds in series.
  • Quench between beds by injecting cold feed straight into the vessel — one shell, no exchanger.
  • Cheaper than configuration 2, but the feed is diluted and the mixing at each injection must be good.
  • The duty leaves through the wall, so the area you can buy is the ceiling.
  • Multi-tubular, built like a shell-and-tube exchanger: $A \lesssim 1000$ m², about 2 500 kW.
  • Stirred tank: standard geometry gives $A/V = 5/D$, and a jacket rarely exceeds 50 m².
  • Excess reactant or an inert diluent raises $\sum F_i C_{p,i}$, so the same $\Delta H_r$ moves the temperature less.
  • Nothing new inside the reactor; the bill arrives as recycle, separation and pumping.
  • Split the feed over $N$ identical isothermal units, each one inside its own area limit.
  • It buys area by buying vessels, so it is the most expensive answer and the last one considered.

1 is where you start and 6 is where you stop. Between them, 2 to 5 are alternatives rather than a ranking: capital cost, operability, safety and the load left to the separation section decide which one wins. Real reactors are often a blend of two.

Lecture 8-3 · between the rungs

Blends, and two rules of thumb for the order

A blend of 1 and 4 · partial removal or addition of heat
  • Part of the duty crosses the wall, the rest leaves in the stream.
  • Neither adiabatic nor isothermal — a partial removal or addition of heat.
  • Size the wall so the outlet still rises no more than 10 % of the inlet.
Judged by the heat of reaction $|\Delta H_r|$
1<2/3/4/5
  • Configuration 1 takes the smallest heat of reaction.
  • 2 to 5 are the answers as $|\Delta H_r|$ grows.
Judged by the heat load $\dot Q_R = F\,\Delta H_r$
1<2/3/4/5<6
  • Multiply by the flow and a second ceiling appears.
  • Only the total duty — never $\Delta H_r$ alone — forces reactors in parallel.

Lecture 8-3 · the one equation

The heat load leaves by two doors

$$\dot Q_R = \dot Q_1 + \dot Q_2$$
$$\dot Q_1 = UA\,(\mathrm{MTD}) \qquad \dot Q_2 = \textstyle\sum_i F_i C_{p,i}(T_{out}-T_{in})$$

On the utility side, $\dot Q_1 = F_{media}C_{p,media}(t_{out}-t_{in})$.

$\dot Q_1$
heat crossing the wall to a utility
kW
$\dot Q_2$
heat leaving in the stream, as a temperature change
kW
$U$, $A$, MTD
coefficient, area, mean temperature difference
W/(m²·K), m², °C

Use the outlet composition in $\sum F_i C_{p,i}$.

Configuration$\dot Q_1$ through the wall$\dot Q_2$ in the stream
1Single adiabatic reactorzerocarries everything
2Adiabatic beds in series + external heating/coolingzero in a bed; all of it in the exchangers betweencarries the load in each bed, reset between beds
3Adiabatic beds in series + cold shotzeroeverything, plus the quench mass injected
4Single isothermal + heating/cooling systemeverything, capped by the $UA$ you can buyzero
5Single adiabatic + excess reactant or inertzeroeverything, but spread over more mass
6Isothermal reactors in paralleleverything, over $N$ walls instead of onezero
  • Read the table as a menu, not a ranking.
  • 1 and 6 are the two ends: nothing through the wall, and everything through $N$ walls.
  • Any of 2 to 5 may be the right answer — the process decides which.

Configuration 1 of 6 · the form and the test

1Single adiabatic reactor

Adiabatic fixed bed: catalyst between layers of inert balls, nothing but a shell (Lecture 9)

Choose it when
  • $|\Delta H_r|$ is small enough that the whole load can leave as a temperature change.
  • The outlet still sits inside the safe, selective, catalyst-tolerant window.
  • An empty vessel: no heat-transfer surface, no utility, no control loop.
It runs out when
  • The adiabatic rise carries the outlet past a selectivity, catalyst or metallurgy limit.

HDA case640 → 766.73 °C, a 19.8 % rise against a 704 °C ceiling. Fails.

Configuration 1 · the guideline

When is an adiabatic reactor acceptable?

  • Exothermic: rise below 10–15 % of the inlet temperature in °C.
  • Endothermic: no guideline — use the experimental minimum.
  • Measured limits beat the percentage whenever data exist.

The guideline is a proxy for catalyst damage, selectivity loss and materials of construction.

A percentage is never the real constraint.

Configuration 1 · the equation

Nothing through the wall, so the stream heats up

The heat balance$\dot Q_R = \dot Q_1 + \dot Q_2$, with $\dot Q_1 = UA(\mathrm{MTD})$
$\dot Q_1 = 0$ no utility, no area — the wall is insulated
$\dot Q_R = \dot Q_2 = \sum_i F_i C_{p,i}(T_{in}-T_{out})$ the whole load must appear as a temperature change
$$T_{out} = T_{in} - \frac{\dot Q_R}{\sum_i F_i C_{p,i}}$$

Exothermic means $\dot Q_R < 0$, so $T_{out} > T_{in}$: the reactor runs away from its inlet temperature.

Configuration 4 of 6 · the opposite extreme of 1

4Single isothermal reactor + heating/cooling system

Multitubular phthalic anhydride reactor: catalyst in the tubes, boiling water on the shell (Lecture 9)

Choose it when
  • The reaction demands one fixed temperature: selectivity, catalyst life or equilibrium.
  • The duty fits the wall that can be bought — multi-tubular $A \lesssim 1000$ m², about 2 500 kW; a stirred-tank jacket rarely passes 50 m².
It runs out when
  • The area the duty demands is larger than one shell can hold.

HDA case8 081 kW needs $A \approx$ 3 230 m² — over three times a single unit. Fails.

Configuration 4 · the equation

Hold the temperature, and the wall does all the work

The heat balance$\dot Q_R = \dot Q_1 + \dot Q_2$
$T_{out} = T_{in} \;\Rightarrow\; \dot Q_2 = \sum_i F_i C_{p,i}(T_{in}-T_{out}) = 0$ no temperature change means no sensible-heat term
$\dot Q_R = \dot Q_1 = UA\,(\mathrm{MTD})$ the entire load must cross the wall
So the question becomes: is there enough area to pass 8 000 kW?

Configuration 4 · the numbers

What a tubular and a tank reactor can pass

TubularTank
$U$ (W/m²·°C)≈ 100≈ 500
$A_{max}$ (m²)≈ 1 000≈ 50
MTD (°C)10 – 2510 – 25
$\dot Q_{1,max}$ (kW)≈ 2 500≈ 700

Tubular: the tube bundle is the heat-transfer area

Take MTD as the log-mean, to start
$\mathrm{LMTD} = \dfrac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln\!\left(\Delta T_1/\Delta T_2\right)}$

Name the utility and both end differences are fixed, so LMTD follows. Good while $A \le 1000$ m² or $\dot Q_1 \le 2500$ kW.

Why a tank runs out of wall

Standard geometry gives $A/V = 5/D$: the wall per unit volume falls as the tank grows, and a jacket rarely exceeds 50 m². Higher $U$, far less area — so it loses.

Configuration 4 · the high-temperature exception

When the duty, not the area, sets the size

An endothermic reaction at 700–900 °C has no utility hot enough to drive it through a jacket. The heat comes from a flame in a furnace box, and the vendor rates that box in kW of duty — there is no $UA(\mathrm{LMTD})$ to size against.

Configuration 2 of 6 · between the two extremes

2Adiabatic beds in series + external heating/cooling

Four adiabatic beds with an exchanger after each — ammonia and methanol converters (Lecture 9)

Choose it when
  • One bed overshoots, but $N$ smaller bites each stay inside the limit.
  • The temperature can be reset between beds in an ordinary exchanger.
  • The interstage duty is a clean hot stream worth recovering.
It runs out when
  • $N-1$ exchangers, extra pressure drop and a taller structure have to be paid for.

HDA caseTwo beds, each stopped at 704 °C, cover the same conversion. Works.

Configuration 2 · split the duty

Let each section take a bite of the heat

One bed rises 127 °C and one wall cannot pass 8 000 kW. Cut the bed into sections and cool between them.

Each bed is adiabatic; the heat exchangers between them carry the load in pieces.

Configuration 2 · the hardware

Circulate, jacket, coil — or intercool

  • Mildly exothermic: external cooler, jacket, or cooling coils.
  • Mildly endothermic: the same three, heated instead.
  • Strongly exothermic: intercoolers between adiabatic stages.

Configuration 2 · sizing the beds

How much conversion goes in each bed?

  • Single reversible reaction: take each section to about 90 % of its equilibrium conversion.
  • Anything more complex: you need the rate law of every reaction.
Hydrodealkylation has four reactions, so the bed count that follows comes from the kinetics and the temperature limit, not from a rule of thumb.

Configuration 2 · interactive

How many beds does the 704 °C limit force?

Adiabatic rise per bed$\Delta T_{bed} = \dfrac{|\dot Q_R|}{N \sum F_i C_{p,i}}$

Two beds is the smallest number that keeps every section below 704 °C — which is exactly what the flowsheet shows.

Configuration 3 of 6 · the form and the test

3Adiabatic beds in series + external mass (cold shot)

The same beds, quenched by cold feed injected between them — SO₃ and hydrotreaters (Lecture 9)

Choose it when
  • A cold stream is already available — fresh feed, or recycle gas.
  • One shell, no exchanger, no interstage piping: cheaper than configuration 2.
It runs out when
  • Dilution costs conversion or selectivity, or the mixing at each injection is poor.

HDA caseQuench with cold recycle gas between the beds — no interstage exchanger at all.

Configuration 3 · cold shots in practice

Quenching between the beds

A cold shot cools and dilutes at once — but it lowers conversion per bed.

Configuration 5 of 6 · the form and the test

5Single adiabatic reactor + external mass

Excess reactant, or an inert diluent, recycled around the reactor as the heat sink (Lecture 9)

Choose it when
  • $|\Delta H_r|$ is high and the temperature must come down without any wall.
  • Extra $\sum F_i C_{p,i}$ can come from excess reactant, an inert diluent, or a recycle the process already carries.
It runs out when
  • Every kilogram added is paid for downstream: larger vessels, more separation, more pumping and compression.

HDA case+20 kW/K of extra heat capacity holds the rise to 15 % — and the recycle gas was already there.

Configuration 5 · add mass

Give the heat more mass to warm up

Adiabatic with an added stream$\dot Q_2 = \sum_i F_i C_{p,i}(T_{in}-T_{out}) + F_m C_{p,m}(T_{m,in}-T_{out})$

Excess reactant

  • Feed more of one reactant than stoichiometry needs

Recycle

  • Return reactant or product from downstream

Inert or cold shot

  • Add a heat carrier
  • Or inject cold feed between beds

$F_m$, $C_{p,m}$ = flow and heat capacity of the added stream, entering at $T_{m,in}$.

Configuration 5 · choosing the carrier

Four things a heat carrier must be

  • Inert — it must not react.
  • Miscible with reactants and products.
  • Easy to separate downstream.
  • High heat capacity per unit mass.
Styrene from ethylbenzene uses 10 moles of steam per mole of feed.

Steam works because water and hydrocarbons separate again after condensation.

Configuration 5 · the three arrangements

Three ways to put the extra mass in

excess reactant · inert diluent · cold shots

Excess reactant — recovered in the separator and recycled. The extra mass is a species the process already handles, so nothing new has to be separated.

Inert diluent — fed with the reactants, separated and returned. S is a foreign component, so it has to be taken out of the product as well.

Cold shots — cold feed injected between the beds. What resets the temperature is mass, not a wall.

Preferred order: recycle a reactant or product first; add a foreign component only when that fails.

Configuration 5 · where the extra mass comes from

Structure I — thirteen streams, two recycles

Before the gas loop was removed, methane and unconverted hydrogen went round and round. That recycle is already a heat carrier — the mass configuration 5 needs is circulating in the plant, unpaid for.

Configuration 6 of 6 · the form and the test

6Isothermal reactors in parallel

One shell is already thousands of tubes in parallel; past its ceiling the plant repeats the shell — common feed header in, common product header out (Lecture 9)

Choose it when
  • The temperature must be held, but the duty is above what one wall can pass.
  • Splitting the feed keeps every reactor under its own area ceiling.
It runs out when
  • $N$ vessels, $N$ control loops, $N$ sets of piping — the most expensive answer on the ladder.

HDA case8 081 kW at 2 500 kW per unit forces 4 reactors in parallel.

Configuration 6 · the sizing

How many units, and why all the same size

One wall has a ceiling, from configuration 4$\dot Q_{max}\approx UA_{max}(\mathrm{MTD}) \approx 2\,500\ \text{kW per multi-tubular shell}$
$$N = \left\lceil \frac{\dot Q_R}{\dot Q_{max}} \right\rceil \qquad \dot Q_{unit}=\frac{\dot Q_R}{N} \qquad A_{unit} = \frac{A_{total}}{N}$$
Reactor duty $\dot Q_R$ (kW)Units at ≤ 2 500 kWArea each (m²)Duty each (kW)
2 50011 0002 500
5 00021 0002 500
8 081 — this reactor48082 020
Guideline · make every unit identical
  • Split the feed evenly, so each unit takes $\dot Q_R/N$ — here 2 020 kW at 808 m², not one at 2 500 and one at 580.
  • Cost: one design, one set of drawings, one fabrication run — and the shells are quoted at a multiple-unit price.
  • Spares: one tube bundle, one gasket set, one spare pump fits every unit.
  • Control: identical units sit at the same temperature and pressure drop, so one control scheme and one set of alarm limits serves all of them.
  • Turndown: take a whole unit off line and the rest stay at their design point; a mismatched set has no clean step.

Parallel buys area by buying vessels: $N$ shells, $N$ control loops, $N$ sets of piping. That is why it sits last on the ladder.

Lecture 8-3 · the whole argument

Choosing the thermal operation of a tubular reactor

One route through the menu. The three middle questions can be asked in any order — a plant that must not be shut down for catalyst change may reach for 4 or 6 long before it considers beds in series.

Lecture 8-3 · summary

What section 8-3 settled

  • Every choice is one heat balance: $\dot Q_R = \dot Q_1 + \dot Q_2$, with one term switched off.
  • Adiabatic fails when the rise exceeds 10 % of the inlet temperature.
  • Single isothermal fails when the duty needs more wall than one shell has.
  • Beds in series split the rise; added mass flattens it. Both fix the same 19.8 %.
8-4

Class activity

Lactic acid from bio-glycerol — the thermal question, marked

Problem II — midterm examination 2025 · lactic acid from bio-glycerol

Reaction and experimental reactor information

  1. Gas–liquid–solid reaction with air as the oxidant in a CSTR (continuous stirred-tank reactor).
  2. Operating target: 150 °C, 10 bara — high enough to keep the water liquid.
  3. Crude glycerol is purified to an aqueous solution of 80 wt % glycerol and 20 wt % water.
  4. Air (20 mol % O₂, 79 mol % N₂, 1 mol % CO₂) is supplied at 200 % excess oxygen relative to the stoichiometry of the main reaction at the reactor inlet.
1. Draw the input–output diagram and give every stream a destination code. 2. Perform the overall material balance for 60,000 t/y of glycerol feed.

Problem II · three routes compete for the same glycerol

Reaction information at 150 °C and 10 bar

$$\underset{\text{Glycerol}}{\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}_3}+\tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_2\rightarrow\underset{\text{Lactic acid}}{\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_3}+\text{H}_2\text{O}\qquad \Delta H=-280\qquad(1)$$
$$\underset{\text{Glycerol}}{\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}_3}+\text{O}_2\rightarrow\underset{\text{Glyceric acid}}{\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_4}+\text{H}_2\text{O}\qquad \Delta H=-456\qquad(2)$$
$$\underset{\text{Glycerol}}{\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}_3}+3.5\,\text{O}_2\rightarrow 3\,\text{CO}_2+4\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\qquad \Delta H=-1567\qquad(3)$$

$\Delta H$ in kJ per mole of glycerol. Single-pass conversion 95 %; selectivities 63 / 22 / 15 mol %.

Problem II · the rest of the reactor information, and what it forces you to assume

Design basis and assumptions

  1. Single-pass glycerol conversion 95 %. On converted glycerol the selectivities are lactic acid (LA) 63 %, glyceric acid (GA) 22 %, complete oxidation 15 mol %.
  2. Reactor feed is held at 20 wt % glycerol, reached by diluting the 80/20 purified feed with deionized water.
  3. Glycerol decomposes at its normal boiling point, so vacuum distillation at 0.30 bara, where it boils at 235 °C, recovers it for recycle.
  • Basis: 60,000 t/y of the purified feed, so 48,000 t/y of glycerol.
  • Steady state, and item 7 means glycerol is recycled to extinction — overall conversion is 1.
  • Item 4 fixes the oxygen at the reactor, not at the process boundary.
  • Oxygen leaves through a vent, so the process excess is a result, not a choice.

Problem II · question 2 · what the marking found

Three mistakes that cost most of the marks

The dilution water

  • More than 80 % of answers never fed water to bring the reactor feed to 20 wt % glycerol
  • 190,105 t/y — the largest single feed in the plant

Which reaction sets the oxygen

  • Stoichiometric oxygen is taken on reaction (1) only, not on all three
  • The excess is quoted against that number

The process excess

  • Assuming 0 % or 10 % at the boundary is wrong here
  • Oxygen is vented, so the boundary excess is whatever the reactor and recycle leave — 216 %

Problem II · question 4 · step 2

What happens if nobody takes the heat out

$$\Delta T=\frac{\dot Q_R}{\sum_i F_iC_{p,i}}=\frac{9\,270}{38.82}=238.8\ \text{K}\qquad T_{out}=150+238.8=388.8\ ^\circ\text{C}$$
$$\text{percent increase}=\frac{388.8-150}{150}=159\ \%$$
159 %sixteen times the 10 % guideline — configuration 1 is not available for this reactor

And 388.8 °C is not merely hot. At 10 bar water boils at 180 °C, so the liquid phase — the reaction medium itself, and 81 % of the heat capacity — would be gone long before the reactor reached it.

Problem II · question 4 · the answer

Isothermal, and then check the wall

Ruled out
  • 1 — single adiabatic: 159 % rise, and the water boils.
  • 2 and 3 — beds in series: a slurry catalyst in a stirred tank is not a packed bed; there are no beds to stage.
Already in the design
  • 5 — external mass: the feed is deliberately diluted from 80 to 20 wt % glycerol. That water carries 31.6 of the 38.8 kW/K; the 159 % would be far worse without it, and it still is not enough.
4Isothermal CSTR held at 150 °C, the 9 270 kW removed through the wall — then size that wall
  • A jacket rarely exceeds 50 m², so 9 270 kW cannot leave through one.
  • Add internal coils and an external pump-around cooler to buy the area.
  • If the duty still passes one vessel's ceiling, split it — configuration 6, reactors in parallel.

Problem II · question 5 · 20 marks

Design and draw the feed preparation PFD

Everything Lecture 7 taught, on one question. Name the change first, then pick the machine, then draw it.

  • The reactor wants 150 °C and 10 bara, and the water must stay liquid.
  • Air arrives at 1 bar, glycerol and water at 1 bar, and the glycerol recycle at 0.3 bar — below atmospheric, because it comes off a vacuum column.
  • Change pressure before temperature, and mix what is alike before you mix what is not.

Problem II · question 5 · the answer

From blocks to equipment, one unit at a time

Five changes, five machines — air up to 10 bar in a compressor, the three liquids mixed in a drum, the 0.3 bar recycle lifted by its own pump, the mixture pumped to 10 bar, then heated to 150 °C — and last the reactor they all feed. Pressure first, temperature last.

Lecture 8-4 · summary

What the activity settled

  • Order the components by boiling point, then give each a role, a classification and a destination.
  • An excess specified at the reactor is not the excess at the process boundary — 200 % becomes 216 %.
  • The heat load is $\sum_j \xi_j \Delta H_{rxn,j}$, one line per reaction, never a net change.
  • The adiabatic rise is that duty divided by $\sum F_iC_{p,i}$ — and it decides which of the six configurations you are allowed to build.

Wrap-up

Key Takeaways

1

Get the heat load first — every thermal decision hangs on that one number.

2

Quote a duty with its operating hours, or the kilowatts mean nothing.

3

Six configurations: 1 first, then any of 2–5 as the context decides, and 6 last.

4

Adiabatic needs a rise inside 10 % of the inlet; one isothermal shell stops near 2 500 kW.

5

Fix a temperature problem with a stream you already have.
